replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper355 by Reviewer RJDm

content.title: For Reviewer RJDm
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,
 
We have clarified the experimental settings and implementation details of our paper. Although we have decided to withdraw the paper, we hope you can post your feedback and we are glad to answer further questions if needed.
 
> Q1: Any code is available online? Looks like UPT can be built on CLIP with moderate efforts.
 
Our implementation is based on CoOp’s code. We will release the code and model to facilitate future research.
 
> Q2: Could you please explain more about the experimental settings of Fig (1)? Some descriptions are confusing to me. For example, on page 2 first paragraph: ‘if the text classifiers are established based on text embeddings of low separability, tuning visual prompts would lend little help to improve the final performance’? Why VPT is affected by this factor since by default VPT doesn’t take any text as input?
 
We apply the VPT into the vision-language field, e.g., CLIP. Similar to Eq.(1), the final prediction of VPT is computed by the cosine similarity of text embeddings $W$ and visual embeddings $z$. For VPT, the visual embeddings $z$ is learnable by injecting extra visual prompts $V$, but the text embeddings $W$ is frozen. For some datasets with small inter-class text variance ($W$ of low separability), merely tuning visual prompts to affect $z$ lend little help to improve the final performance. Fig. 2(g) and our discussion in section 2.2 are helpful for understanding.
 
> Q3: How do you split text/ visual prompts after the transformer layer?
 
We just use the basic `torch.split` operator. For example, for the tensor $\hat{U}$ of shape $[8, d]$, we split the front part to get text prompts $\hat{U_{t}} \in [4, d]$, and split the rear part to get the visual prompts $\hat{U_{v}} \in [4, d]$.
 
> Q4: Any explanation about why shared prompts in Fig(5b) perform worst, but the proposed UPT works fine (the difference is the shared prompts in UPT are transformed with self-attention)?
 
Shared prompts method (Fig 5b) means the learnable prompts $U$ are optimized for both text and visual modalities. But the essential differences existing between these two modalities, e.g., the optimal solution for parameter weights of different modalities could be different. Thus, directly using $U$ for all the modalities is not an ideal choice. For our UPT, starting with the unified prompt $U$, we use the self-attention layer to get the $\hat{U}$ and split $\hat{U}$ to text prompts $\hat{U_{t}}$ and visual prompts $\hat{U_{v}}$. Compared with the shared prompts approach, the experimental results show that our `separation` design is more effective.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Current papers on prompt learning have mostly focused on language prompting (using prompting on the language branch of CLIP). Recent work has proposed instead to apply prompting to the visual branch. The current work proposes a way to do prompting on both branches simultaneously by means of a set of prompts to which each branch attends to with independent attention mechanisms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The paper is very clear
- The results are interesting, improving performance against the main baselines.
- Prompting is an interesting tool that is getting a lot of attention lately.

Cons:
- The method is a bit incremental
- Motivation through correlations between intra- and inter- class variance with each of the prompting techniques is a bit weak. The correlation plot does not show a very clear signal, and no strong intuition of why that would be the case is given.
- Results: 
1) I don't know exactly where the base results are from. I have checked a few of the references and the numbers do not match up. The trends do, and I'm sure it is just some differences on the experimental setting that are well justified. But still, just for the purpose of clarity, it would be nice to see where they are taken from (or if the authors re-run the authors code). 
2) There does not seem to be a distinction from base and new classes. Is this the case? is there a reason?
3) CoOp has been superseded by CoCoOp, and ProDa also shows strong results. Shouldn't these be included somehow? they are CVPR'22.
4) I think the cross-dataset experiment is an interesting one (Table 2 on CoCoOp) and would be a nice add.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very clear in terms of methodology, competing methods, reasoning, etc. An easy read.

The paper is somewhat interesting, although somewhat incremental. The technical contribution of having some tokens that each branch attends to is ok but not superb, and some exploration of alternatives is also reasonable work. Overall reasonable work.

There's some details that could provide a bit extra reproducibility, but overall the method is quite simple. The authors also state they will release code.

content.title: For Reviewer d8Y6
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,
 
We have clarified the novelty, motivation, and experimental setting of our paper. Although we have decided to withdraw the paper, we hope you can post your feedback and we are glad to answer further questions if needed.
 
> Q1: The method is a bit incremental
 
We argue that previous prompt tuning methods merely focus on single modality, while we first present a unified prompt method to tune both the visual and text modalities. We think the findings presented in the paper and our neat design can be useful for the community to investigate more advanced multi-modal designs for adapting large pre-trained VL models.
 
> Q2: Motivation through correlations between intra- and inter- class variance with each of the prompting techniques is a bit weak. The correlation plot does not show a very clear signal, and no strong intuition of why that would be the case is given.

We recommend combining the correlation plot and our 3D ball visualization to understand our intuition. We provide a comprehensive analysis in section 2.2. Note that reviewer ww1n thinks our motivation is informative and well-motivated.
 
> Q3: I don't know exactly where the base results are from. I have checked a few of the references and the numbers do not match up. The trends do, and I'm sure it is just some differences on the experimental setting that are well justified. But still, just for the purpose of clarity, it would be nice to see where they are taken from (or if the authors re-run the authors code).
 
We have three baselines (CoOp, CoCoOp, VPT shallow/deep) and two settings (few-shot learning and domain generalization). For VPT shallow/deep, we obtain their results by adapting their source code (https://github.com/KMnP/vpt) to CoOp’s code. For the few-shot learning setting (Figure 4 and Table 2 in our paper), we re-run the code of CoOp with the CoCoOp’s initialization setting. Specifically, we fix the text prompt length to 4 and initialize the text prompts using the pre-trained word embeddings of “a photo of a”. Note that with the advanced initialization setting, our re-run results are higher than the origin results in CoOp. For the domain generalization setting (Table 1 in our paper), the results of CoOp and CoCoOp are copied from Table 3 of CoCoOp.
  
> Q5: CoOp has been superseded by CoCoOp, and ProDa also shows strong results. Shouldn't these be included somehow? they are CVPR'22.
 
We cannot directly compare with ProDA because the backbones and datasets reported in ProDA are different from ours, and we do not find the official public code of ProDA. We try our best to re-implement the code of ProDA and get a similar precision under their setting. We have added the comparison with ProDA based on our re-implemented results. We find that even compared with the strong baseline ProDA, UPT still boosts the accuracy of 0.11/1.01/0.67/1.5/1.61(\%) on 1/2/4/8/16 few shot settings. 
 
> Q4 & Q6: There does not seem to be a distinction from base and new classes. Is this the case? is there a reason? I think the cross-dataset experiment is an interesting one (Table 2 on CoCoOp) and would be a nice add.
 
In the main paper, our experimental setting follows CoOp (few-shot learning, domain generalization) rather than CoCoOp (base to new generalization, cross-dataset transfer). We think the CoOp’s setting is already widely used in many follow ups (e.g, the ProDA paper you mentioned) and is enough to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
Also, we acknowledge the CoCoOp’s setting is another interesting research topic that focuses on the generalization ability of prompt tuning approaches. We have included the CoCoOp’s setting in the appendix, and find that our UPT still outperforms previous baselines such as CoCoOp.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a unified vision and language prompt learning method for the CLIP model. Different from prior work (VPT and COOP), the proposed method learn a tiny neural network to jointly optimize the prompt across different modalities. The authors did some study on different prompt methods and found sub-optimal performance due to intrinsic discrepancy between text the image modalities. Experiment results verify the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

- The paper points out the problem of VPT and COOP with visualization on different downstream datasets, which is informative and well-motivated (Figure 2).

- the transformer adaptor seems to be working really well; without the transformer adapter, the proposed joint training is not working well. 

- The proposed solution seems to perform well on the evaluated benchmark. There is a huge boost over the few-shot evaluation. 

[Weaknesses]

- The proposed approaches basically combine the VPT and COOP methods with joint training and use a transformer to learn the prompt. I have a little bit of concern with the overall novelness of the paper if we only consider the joint training. From table 2, it seems the main benefit comes from the transformer model used in the model since non of the other ablations works better compared to the baseline model. However, the reason behind this is only with limited discussion. 

- In table 1, the author only compared two baseline models. none of the variants of VPT and COOP methods has been compared in the table. 

- Why MLP and joint training is even worse compared to the baseline methods? Does joint training with vision and language always outperform training with single modalities? 

- In the proposed method (UPT), there are three datasets that perform worse than the baseline. I wonder what the reason behind this is. why MLP model performs well on these three tasks? Is there any analysis and plot that can reveal the reason?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There are some missing details in the paper, such as hyperparams for the transformer model and all the ablations. Without releasing the code, the result might be hard to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed to jointly combine VPT and COOP for prompt learning and shows with the transformer adaptor, the result is much better compared to the baseline. However, as I pointed out in the weakness session, the real reason behind the improvements is not clear to me and the paper is lack of comparison with more recent related methods.

content.title: For Reviewer ww1n
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

We have clarified the novelty of our paper. Although we have decided to withdraw the paper, we hope you can post your feedback and we are glad to answer further questions if needed.

> Q1: I have a little bit of concern with the overall novelness of the paper if we only consider the joint training. From table 2, it seems the main benefit comes from the transformer model used in the model since none of the other ablations works better compared to the baseline model. However, the reason behind this is only with limited discussion.
 
We have three single-modal baselines (CoOp, VPT-shallow and VPT-deep) and we present three ablation choices of multi-modal training – joint training, shared, MLP. Also, we have two experimental settings - few-shot learning and domain generalization. Does none of the other ablations work better compared to the baselines? This is not true. For the few-shot setting, if we consider the average results over 11 datasets, joint training and MLP outperform the CoOp baseline. All the ablation methods beat the VPT-shallow, but are worse than the VPT-deep baseline. VPT-deep has a large number of parameters and achieves strong performance in the few-shot learning setting but obtains poorest performance in the domain generalization setting. We also update the results of three ablation approaches on the domain generalization setting, and we find that all of them perform better than the VPT-deep baseline. We think the comparison between ablation methods and CoOp/VPT can show that multi-modal prompt tuning still helps. But due to the intrinsic discrepancy between text and image modalities, we should carefully select an appropriate way to generate the prompts of different modalities. Our advanced self-attention based UPT beats all the single-modal baselines including VPT-deep on few-shot learning and domain generalization benchmarks. 
 
> Q2: In table 1, the author only compared two baseline models. none of the variants of VPT and COOP methods has been compared in the table.
 
We add the comparison with ProDA - a recent follow-up paper of CoOp in our revised version. VPT is already the latest published work for visual prompt tuning. If you think there are other published papers we need to compare, please specify their names and thanks.
We would like to emphasize that our method is the first prompt tuning method that considers optimization on both textual and visual modalities. We provide a neat pipeline that is easy for others to follow. Recent prompt tuing papers still focus on single modality. For example, ProDA designs more sophisticated loss functions, but do not affect the CLIP visual features. Our method can be combined with these single-modal follow-ups (e.g., we can also add the loss of ProDA to our text prompt tuning branch) and may further improve the performance, but we want to keep our clean pipeline and leave for future research.
 
> Q3: Why MLP and joint training is even worse compared to the baseline methods? Does joint training with vision and language always outperform training with single modalities?

This question is related to Q1. For the few-shot setting, if we consider the average results over 11 datasets, the MLP and joint training outperform single-modality baselines CoOp and VPT-shallow. Even compared with the strong VPT-deep baseline, MLP achieves better performance on 4 of 11 datasets. VPT-deep beats MLP and joining training approaches by using more prompt parameters, which will affect the generalizability. On the domain generalization setting, MLP/joint training beat all the single-modal baselines. So we think MLP/joint training approaches could show the advantages of multi-modal prompt tuning approaches. We cannot say “always outperform”. According to the `no free lunch theorem` and Fig 1 in our motivation, the data distribution of different datasets matters. UPT performs better in most datasets than the single-modal baseline, which is enough to show the effectiveness of our method.
 
> Q4: In the proposed method, there are three datasets that perform worse than the baseline. I wonder what the reason behind this is. why MLP model performs well on these three tasks? Is there any analysis and plot that can reveal the reason?
 
According to Table 2, UPT does not achieve best performance on three datasets: OxfordPets, Food101 and EuroSAT. For the OxfordPets and Food101 datasets, we explain the reasons in the bottom part of section 3.1. Specifically, these two datasets contain noisy training data with intense colors and sometimes wrong labels that will interfere with the training of prompt tuning models. The MLP model has a smaller number of parameters and suffers less interference. As for the EuroSAT datasets, our method performs a little worse than the MLP baseline (90.51 vs 90.66) and we think this gap is small. Overall, our UPT achieves the state-of-the-art on 8 over 11 datasets, and we think the overall experimental results are enough.
